text: Role-based access, least privilege, segregation of duties, access reviews, privileged access, every lesson in this chapter is a control. Access governance is the program that decides when each control fires and who's accountable. This lesson sets up that coordinating layer.

Most access changes trace back to one of three lifecycle events. Joiner, a new hire needs a starting set of access tied to their role. Mover, someone changes teams and needs new access, and critically, needs their old access removed. Leaver, someone's employment ends and all access gets revoked, fast enough that a Friday termination doesn't leave an active login over the weekend. Mover is where programs most often fail quietly, granting new access is easy to remember, removing the old access is nobody's trigger unless governance makes it one.

Every access decision involves four roles. The requester identifies a business need. The approver, typically the data or system owner, decides whether the request is justified. The provisioner, a person or an automated workflow, actually executes the grant. The auditor, independent of the first three, later confirms the grant was approved, provisioned correctly, and is still appropriate. The same person shouldn't request, approve, and grant their own access with nobody else involved.

A well-run access governance program doesn't invent new controls, it schedules and documents the ones this chapter covers: role-based starting access, a least-privilege check before approval, no single workflow letting one person both request and approve, a review cadence, extra scrutiny for admin accounts. Without that layer, an organization can have every individual control in place and still fail an audit, because nobody can produce evidence of when and why each grant happened.
Four questions, every system: who can request, who approves, who provisions, who audits. Next up: role-based access control, the first control this governance layer schedules.
